name: Selenium
occurrence: Rare, dispersed in sulfide ores and recovered mainly as a by-product of copper refining.
biologicalRelevance: An essential trace nutrient and component of the antioxidant enzyme glutathione peroxidase, though the safe dose range is unusually narrow — both deficiency and excess cause health problems.
notableCharacteristics: Its electrical conductivity changes dramatically when exposed to light, which is exactly what made it useful in early photocopiers and light meters.
ncertRelevance: trace nutrient with narrow safe range
whyHere: Named after the Greek moon goddess Selene (as a partner to tellurium, named for Earth), selenium sits just below sulfur and shares its tendency to form -2 and +6 states, but its greater atomic size gives it useful photoconductive behaviour sulfur lacks.
didYouKnow: Selenium's conductivity increases measurably under light exposure, a property discovered by accident in 1873 when a technician noticed a selenium resistor behaved oddly on a sunny day — it kicked off the entire field of photoconductivity.
genZNote: Named after the moon goddess and reacts to actual light. The most main-character origin story on this list.
